title: Drawing a Snake and Adding Feet
text:
A nobleman of Chu, after making a sacrifice, gave his retainers a jug of wine. There was not enough for all of them, but it was too much for one. So they agreed on a contest: each would draw a snake on the ground, and whoever finished first would drink the whole jug.

One man finished his snake quickly. He picked up the jug and was about to drink, but seeing that the others were still drawing, he held the wine in his left hand and with his right began to add feet to his snake, to show how fast and clever he was.

Before he had finished the feet, another man completed his snake and snatched the jug from him. A snake has no feet, he said. How can you give it feet? And he drank the wine. The man who drew the feet lost the prize.

The adviser Chen Zhen told this story to Zhao Yang, a Chu general who had just won a great victory over Wei and was now preparing to attack Qi. He already held the highest rank, Chen argued. A new war could add nothing to it, but defeat could take away everything he had won. Zhao Yang saw the point, and withdrew his army.
lesson: Once you have won, know when to stop. Extra flourishes after the job is done add risk without adding value, and can cost you the victory.
people: Chen Zhen, Zhao Yang, retainers of a Chu nobleman
source: Zhanguo Ce (Strategies of the Warring States), Qi section
